Friday ✅.

📉 The dashboard: The S&P 500 closed down 1.8%.

1 big thing: PC's AI reckoning
By Pete Gannon
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios
 

Intel sent investors scrambling with a stark warning about the sharpening slowdown in the personal computer market.

Why it matters: AI is helping fuel the slowdown — driving up the price of PCs and competing for crucial IT budgets — and causing an industrywide rethink for what personal computers may look like down the road.

The big picture: The PCs most of us know today — used primarily for web browsing, running software and other everyday tasks — could look radically different in an AI-driven world.

  • "How we think about the personal computer will very likely change," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in June while unveiling a new chip platform for an AI-powered Windows PC.
  • That sentiment was echoed yesterday on Intel's earnings call, with Intel CFO David Zinsner saying the PC "is going to go through a renaissance despite this [slowdown]."

State of play: Today, PC sales are deteriorating quickly.

  • Intel expects worldwide PC shipments to fall about 12% this year, followed by another roughly 10% decline in 2027.
  • The company, which supplies processors to PC makers like Dell and HP, said Thursday that the pace of that PC "correction" has accelerated over the last two months, and predicted that the market over the next few quarters will be "challenging."

📉 The impact: Intel's stock plummeted over 28%, while Dell, HP and Lenovo fell 10.7%, 9.6% and 7.4%, respectively.

The intrigue: PCs are already evolving.

  • Intel's sales of processors for AI-capable PCs grew 35% in the third quarter compared to a year ago, even as revenue across its broader client computing business fell 5%.
  • Lenovo says it has about a quarter of the global AI PC market and is developing personal AI agents designed to work across multiple devices.
  • HP said AI PCs accounted for 46% of its unit shipments last quarter, a share the company expects to reach 60%–70% next year.

The bottom line: "Before you get to the future you have to live through the present," Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon wrote Friday in a note about Intel.

  • Those words could ring true for the PC industry, too.

2. AI's big, ugly week
 
Data: FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips

A flood of AI news this week failed to shore up investor confidence in the investment boom driving both the economy and markets, Axios' Matt Phillips writes.

Why it matters: There's basically one story in the markets, and it's AI.

  • The S&P 500's information technology sector — plus hyperscalers Meta, Amazon and Alphabet — now account for over 50% of the market capitalization of the index.

Catch up quick: On Monday, Anthropic's much-awaited investment prospectus arrived, starting the countdown on its IPO, and Meta announced a $95 billion share offering.

  • Wednesday, Microsoft and Alphabet — previously considered perhaps the most stable players in the AI frenzy — reported quarterly earnings.
  • Yesterday, Amazon added its quarterly update to the pile, as did Intel, which has been increasingly swept up in the boom because of growing demand for its CPUs.

State of play: Essentially, every update investors received this week seemed only to stimulate fresh questions and doubt about the boom.

  • The large-cap, tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 stumbled to its third straight weekly loss.
  • So did themed AI ETFs like First Trust Bloomberg Artificial Intelligence.
  • The SOX semiconductor index notched its fourth straight week in the red.

Yes, but: If there was a winner among the AI-pilled parts of the tech sector this week, it was likely Microsoft, which was basically flat for the week after reporting strong results on Tuesday.

  • Unlike its hyperscaling rivals, the results showed that Microsoft is still able to generate positive cash flow thanks, in part, to remarkable stability in its core cloud computing business.

The bottom line: The market's AI issues remain far from resolved.

4. Morning troll
 

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk (left) and Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao. Photos: Britta Pedersen/Pool/AFP via Getty Images; Zed Jameson/Bloomberg via Getty Images
 

Nothing screams Friday like a public spat between billionaires, Pete writes.

  • Driving the news: Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao didn't much appreciate Elon Musk's lack of sensitivity around the $6.3 billion hack on the crypto platform.

🥊 Zoom in: While details of the scale of the attack trickled out last night, Zhao, known as CZ, posted an assurance that Binance would cover the losses.

  • A user replied by pasting an old tweet from convicted FTX chief Sam Bankman-Fried assuring the public that his exchange had the capital to cover customer losses as FTX came apart. (Spoiler alert: It did not.)
  • To that, Musk replied with a grimacing face emoji 😬 — the social media equivalent of yelling "BURN!" while tensions flare at recess.
  • CZ shot back at Musk, saying it was a "bad time to troll," before casually mentioning that Binance controlled over $1 billion in stock in Musk's SpaceX.

💰 The latest: Binance this afternoon said it has set aside the full amount in company funds to cover the lost assets, 80% of which are in the exact impacted token assets. It said it is "actively buying the remaining relevant token assets through market and OTC channels."
